children.name: Polydesmida
Xystodesmidae
Rudiloria
children.description: Rudiloria is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometrid moths or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and belong to a large family of moths whose caterpillars move in a characteristic looping motion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rudiloria moths can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their specific wing markings and coloration patterns that are unique to this genus.
children.funFact: Like other geometrid moths, Rudiloria caterpillars are called 'inchworms' because they arch their bodies into loops when crawling, appearing to measure the ground inch by inch.

children.name: Apheloria
children.description: Apheloria is a genus of large, colorful millipedes known for their striking black bodies with bright yellow, orange, or red markings. These impressive arthropods are among the most recognizable millipedes in eastern North America, often called flat-backed millipedes due to their distinctive body shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipedes, Apheloria species have a notably flattened back and bold warning coloration that advertises their chemical defenses. Their segments are wider and more shield-like compared to the cylindrical bodies of most other millipedes.
children.funFact: When threatened, these millipedes can secrete hydrogen cyanide and other toxic compounds from special glands, making their bright colors a honest warning to potential predators to stay away.

children.name: Howellaria
children.description: Howellaria is a small genus of parasitic wasps that contains only one species found in New England. These tiny insects are specialized parasitoids that develop inside the bodies of other insects, particularly targeting specific host species during their larval stage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Howellaria wasps are distinguished by their extremely small size and highly specialized parasitic lifestyle, with very specific host preferences that set them apart from other parasitic wasp genera.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, Howellaria wasps play an important role in natural pest control by helping to regulate populations of their insect hosts.

children.name: Boraria
children.description: Boraria is a small genus of marine bryozoans, tiny colonial animals that live in encrusting communities on hard surfaces like rocks and shells. These filter-feeding creatures build intricate calcium carbonate structures that look like delicate lacework when viewed up close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boraria species are distinguished by their distinctive box-like zooids (individual colony members) arranged in regular patterns, with characteristic pore structures that differ from other encrusting bryozoans.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Boraria are often mistaken for corals or even plants due to their branching, plant-like growth patterns.

children.name: Pleuroloma
children.description: Pleuroloma is a small genus of millipedes found in eastern North America. These cylindrical, many-legged creatures are part of the larger group of julid millipedes, which are known for their ability to roll into tight spirals when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pleuroloma millipedes can be identified by their specific body segment structure and the arrangement of their defensive glands along their sides.
children.funFact: The single New England species, the Traveling Cherry Millipede, gets its common name from its reddish-brown coloration and its tendency to wander widely through forest leaf litter.

children.description: Cherry millipedes are a distinctive family of colorful millipedes found throughout New England's forests. These segmented arthropods are known for their striking warning colors - typically bright reds, oranges, or yellows combined with black - that advertise their ability to produce defensive chemicals when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipede families, cherry millipedes have flattened bodies with prominent keeled segments and display vivid aposematic (warning) coloration. They also possess specialized glands that can secrete hydrogen cyanide as a defense mechanism.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, cherry millipedes smell like almonds when handled because they release hydrogen cyanide, the same compound that gives bitter almonds their distinctive scent.

children.name: Polydesmidae
Pseudopolydesmus
children.description: Pink Flat-backs are a small group of millipedes known for their distinctive flattened bodies and pinkish coloration. These soil-dwelling creatures are typically found in leaf litter and rotting wood throughout New England forests, where they help break down organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their cylindrical millipede relatives, Pink Flat-backs have notably flattened, wedge-shaped bodies that allow them to squeeze into tight spaces between layers of decomposing leaves and bark.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting a rosy hue, Pink Flat-backs can actually range from pale pink to reddish-brown, and their coloration often becomes more vibrant when they're active during humid conditions.

children.name: Polydesmus
children.description: Polydesmus is a genus of flat-backed millipedes that are easily recognized by their distinctive broad, flattened body segments. These small decomposers play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead plant material and enriching the soil. They are typically found under logs, stones, and leaf litter in moist woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have notably wide, flat body segments that extend laterally like small shields, giving them their characteristic pancake-like appearance when viewed from above.
children.funFact: Despite being called millipedes, Polydesmus species typically have only 19-20 pairs of legs, nowhere near the thousand legs their name suggests!

children.description: Polydesmidae is a family of flat-backed millipedes that are among the most common millipedes found crawling through leaf litter and soil in New England forests. These segmented creatures have flattened bodies with broad, wing-like extensions called paranota that stick out from each side of their segments. They play important roles as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike cylindrical millipedes, polydesmids have distinctly flattened bodies with prominent side plates (paranota) that give them their characteristic flat-backed appearance. They also typically have exactly 20 body segments as adults, fewer than many other millipede families.
children.funFact: Despite being called millipedes (meaning 'thousand feet'), these flat-backed millipedes actually have only about 62-66 legs as adults - far fewer than their name suggests!

children.name: Paradoxosomatidae
Oxidus
children.description: Oxidus is a genus of small, slender millipedes that are commonly found in greenhouse environments and warm, moist areas. These millipedes are characterized by their relatively small size and pale coloration, typically measuring less than an inch in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Oxidus are distinguished from other millipedes by their small, delicate build and their preference for human-modified environments like greenhouses and basements rather than natural forest habitats.
children.funFact: The Greenhouse Millipede is actually native to Japan but has become one of the most widely distributed millipedes in the world, hitchhiking in soil and plant shipments to spread across continents.

children.name: Orthomorpha
children.description: Orthomorpha is a genus of millipedes known for their distinctive body structure and defensive capabilities. These segmented creatures have cylindrical bodies with numerous legs and can roll into a tight coil when threatened. They are primarily found in tropical and subtropical regions around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Orthomorpha millipedes are characterized by their prominent lateral flanges (wing-like extensions) along their body segments, which give them a distinctive ridged appearance that sets them apart from other millipede genera.
children.funFact: The Long-flange Millipede is actually native to Southeast Asia but has successfully established populations in New England, making it one of the few tropical millipede species to adapt to our cooler climate.

children.description: Paradoxical keeled millipedes are cylindrical arthropods with distinctive ridges or 'keels' running along the sides of their body segments. These millipedes are typically small to medium-sized and are often found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist soil environments where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The prominent lateral keels (ridges) on their body segments set them apart from other millipede families. Many species in this family also have relatively long legs compared to other millipedes.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting something mysterious, these millipedes got the 'paradoxical' label simply because early taxonomists found their classification puzzling due to their unique combination of physical features.

children.description: Flat-backed millipedes are a diverse group of many-legged arthropods that have distinctively flattened, broad body segments instead of the cylindrical shape of most other millipedes. Each segment typically has wing-like extensions called paranota that give them their characteristic flat appearance. Like all millipedes, they are gentle decomposers that feed on decaying plant matter and help recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike cylindrical millipedes that can roll into a tight ball, flat-backed millipedes have broad, flattened segments with prominent side extensions that prevent them from coiling completely. Their body segments are also typically harder and more armored than those of pill millipedes.
children.funFact: Many flat-backed millipedes, especially the colorful cherry millipedes, produce cyanide as a defense mechanism and advertise their toxicity with bright warning colors like pink, red, or yellow.

children.name: Julida
Julidae
Cylindroiulus
children.description: Barrel millipedes are small, cylindrical arthropods that get their name from their rounded, barrel-like body shape. These gentle decomposers feed on decaying plant matter and organic debris found in soil and leaf litter. They play an important role in breaking down dead vegetation and enriching forest soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike flat-backed millipedes, barrel millipedes have distinctly rounded, cylindrical bodies that can roll into a tight coil when threatened. Their segments are clearly defined with a smooth, glossy appearance.
children.funFact: When disturbed, barrel millipedes can curl up into a perfect spiral, protecting their soft underside while looking like a tiny cinnamon roll!

children.name: Ophyiulus
children.description: Ophyiulus is a genus of snake millipedes, cylindrical creatures that move in snake-like undulating motions through soil and leaf litter. These millipedes are distinguished by their fuzzy, hair-like covering that gives them a distinctive furry appearance. They are detritivores, feeding on decaying organic matter and playing an important role in forest ecosystem nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably hairy or fuzzy exterior, which sets them apart from the smooth-bodied snake millipedes in related genera. Their body segments are also more distinctly separated than in some other snake millipede groups.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'snake millipedes,' they don't actually have a thousand legs - the single New England species typically has around 60-70 pairs of legs that work in coordinated waves to create their serpentine movement.

children.description: Julidae is a family of smooth, cylindrical millipedes that are among the most common millipedes found in New England forests and gardens. These gentle decomposers have long, worm-like bodies divided into many segments, each bearing two pairs of legs that help them navigate through leaf litter and soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their smooth, shiny exoskeleton and lack the defensive glands or spines found in many other millipede families. They typically have a more streamlined appearance compared to their chunkier millipede relatives.
children.funFact: When threatened, these millipedes curl into a tight spiral like a watch spring, protecting their softer underside while presenting their hard back to potential predators.

children.name: Blaniulidae
Blaniulus
children.description: Blaniulus is a genus of small, slender millipedes that are part of the julid family. These cylindrical creatures have numerous body segments and move in a characteristic wave-like motion through soil and leaf litter. They are detritivores, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter and help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Blaniulus are distinguished by their relatively small size, smooth body surface, and distinctive spotted or banded coloration patterns. Unlike some other millipede genera, they lack prominent defensive glands and tend to be more slender in build.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' (meaning 'thousand feet'), Blaniulus species typically have only 30-40 pairs of legs, far short of their name's promise!

children.name: Choneiulus
children.description: Choneiulus is a genus of millipedes that includes species adapted to various habitats across different regions. These segmented creatures are part of the larger millipede family and play important roles in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species known as the Palm Millipede.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Choneiulus can be distinguished from other millipedes by their specific body segmentation patterns and reproductive structures. They typically have a more elongated form compared to some of their millipede relatives.
children.funFact: The Palm Millipede gets its common name from its original discovery in palm houses and greenhouses, where it thrived in the warm, humid conditions that mimicked tropical environments.

children.description: Thin Snake Millipedes are small, slender millipedes that live in soil and leaf litter throughout New England's forests and gardens. These pale, thread-like creatures are much thinner than typical millipedes, earning their snake-like common name from their smooth, elongated bodies that can stretch and coil as they move through tight spaces underground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their chunkier millipede relatives, Thin Snake Millipedes have extremely slender bodies with relatively few segments and a smooth, almost translucent appearance. Their thread-like form allows them to navigate through the tiniest soil pores and crevices.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' (meaning 'thousand feet'), Thin Snake Millipedes typically have fewer than 100 legs, and they can actually stretch their bodies to nearly twice their resting length when squeezing through narrow spaces.

children.name: Parajulidae
Ptyoiulus
children.description: Ptyoiulus is a genus of small, slender millipedes that belong to the family Blaniulidae. These cylindrical creatures have segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per segment and are typically found in leaf litter, soil, and rotting wood where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively small size and distinctive tail-like projection at the rear end, which gives them their common name of 'tailed millipedes.'
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting a thousand legs, Ptyoiulus millipedes actually have far fewer legs, typically ranging from 30 to 90 legs depending on their age and number of body segments.

children.name: Uroblaniulus
children.description: Uroblaniulus is a genus of millipedes known for their distinctive curved tail segments that give them their common name. These small, elongated arthropods are soil-dwelling decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably curved or sickle-shaped posterior segments, which sets them apart from other millipede groups with straight body segments.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' meaning 'thousand feet,' Uroblaniulus canadensis actually has far fewer legs - typically around 30-40 pairs depending on its age and size.

children.description: Parajulid millipedes are small, cylindrical creatures that curl up into a tight spiral when threatened. These soil-dwelling arthropods have numerous body segments, each bearing two pairs of legs, and play an important role in breaking down decaying plant matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other millipede families, parajulids are relatively small and have distinctive reproductive structures and body proportions that help scientists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' (meaning 'thousand feet'), parajulid millipedes actually have far fewer legs - typically between 30-90 pairs depending on the species and their age.

children.description: Snake millipedes are cylindrical, worm-like creatures that get their name from their smooth, serpentine movement as they crawl through soil and leaf litter. These gentle decomposers have hard, segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per segment, and they feed on decaying plant matter, helping to recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems. Unlike their many-legged cousins, snake millipedes have a more streamlined appearance and smoother body surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snake millipedes can be identified by their smooth, cylindrical bodies that lack the pronounced ridges or bumps found on other millipede groups. Their bodies are typically more elongated and snake-like compared to the chunkier, more robust appearance of other millipedes.
children.funFact: When threatened, many snake millipedes can coil into a tight spiral like a watch spring, protecting their soft underside while presenting their hard, armored back to potential predators.

children.name: Chordeumatida
Craspedosomatidae
Craspedosoma
children.description: Craspedosoma is a genus of small millipedes that belong to the family Craspedosomatidae. These tiny arthropods are characterized by their cylindrical, segmented bodies and are typically found in leaf litter and soil where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other millipedes by their relatively small size and specific body segment arrangements, along with unique reproductive structures that are used by experts for identification.
children.funFact: Despite being called millipedes, Craspedosoma species don't actually have a thousand legs - they typically have fewer than 100 legs, with the exact number varying based on how many body segments they possess.

children.description: Craspedosomatidae is a small family of millipedes found in cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere. These cylindrical arthropods are part of the order Chordeumatida and are characterized by their relatively small size and segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per body segment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other millipedes by their unique body structure and the arrangement of their reproductive organs, particularly in males which have specialized gonopods (modified legs used for mating).
children.funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' (meaning 'thousand feet'), species in this family typically have fewer than 60 legs total throughout their entire lives.

children.name: Cleidogonidae
Cleidogona
children.description: Shining Quick Millipedes are small, glossy millipedes known for their relatively fast movement compared to other millipedes. They have smooth, shiny bodies that reflect light, giving them their characteristic gleaming appearance as they navigate through leaf litter and soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These millipedes are distinguished by their notably shiny exoskeleton and quicker locomotion than typical millipedes. Their smooth, polished appearance makes them easily recognizable among the more matte-textured millipede species.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'quick' millipedes, they're still much slower than centipedes - their speed is only impressive compared to other millipedes, which are notoriously slow movers!

children.description: Cleidogonidae is a small family of millipedes known for their distinctive shiny, metallic appearance that gives them their common name of shining quick millipedes. These small arthropods are typically found in soil and leaf litter where they feed on decaying organic matter. They play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their notably glossy, reflective exoskeleton and relatively quick movements compared to other millipedes. They also have a distinctive body shape with well-defined segments and relatively short antennae.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'quick' millipedes, they still move much slower than centipedes and get their name only in comparison to other millipede species that move at an even more leisurely pace.

children.name: Conotylidae
Conotyla
children.description: Winterchill Millipedes are a small genus of millipedes that are specially adapted to survive in cold climates. These hardy arthropods are known for their ability to remain active even in chilly conditions that would slow down most other millipedes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most millipedes that become dormant in cold weather, Conotyla species can tolerate and remain active in much cooler temperatures than their relatives.
children.funFact: These millipedes get their common name from their remarkable cold tolerance - they can often be found crawling around in leaf litter even on frosty autumn mornings when other millipedes have retreated underground.

children.description: Conotylidae is a small family of millipedes that includes some of the most cold-adapted members of their class. These hardy arthropods are built for life in cooler climates and can remain active even in chilly conditions that would slow down most other millipedes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their exceptional cold tolerance and specialized body structures that help them survive in temperate and northern regions where other millipedes struggle.
children.funFact: The name 'Winterchill Millipedes' comes from their remarkable ability to stay active in near-freezing temperatures when most other millipedes have gone dormant for the season.

children.description: Sausage millipedes are small, cylindrical millipedes that get their name from their plump, sausage-like body shape. They are typically found in leaf litter, rotting logs, and soil where they feed on decaying plant matter and help break down organic material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipedes, sausage millipedes have a distinctly swollen, barrel-shaped body that is wider in the middle than at the ends, giving them their characteristic sausage appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being called millipedes (meaning 'thousand feet'), sausage millipedes typically have fewer than 60 legs, with the exact number varying by species and increasing as they molt and grow.

children.name: Polyzoniida
Polyzoniidae
Petaserpes
children.description: Petaserpes is a small genus of millipedes that includes some of the most unusual members of this group. These creatures are known for their ability to retract their head completely into their body segments when threatened, earning them the common name 'slug millipedes' due to their soft, flexible appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most millipedes, Petaserpes species have a soft, expandable body that can change shape dramatically, and they lack the hard, rigid segments typical of other millipedes.
children.funFact: When disturbed, the slug millipede can pull its head so far back into its body that it becomes completely invisible, creating what looks like a headless, slug-like creature.

children.description: Polyzoniidae is a family of millipedes known for their distinctive pill-shaped body form and ability to roll into a tight ball when threatened. These small, dark-colored millipedes have relatively few body segments compared to other millipede families, typically ranging from 17-22 segments. They are found in forest leaf litter and soil where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most millipedes which have long, cylindrical bodies, polyzoniids have a more compact, pill-like shape and can completely roll into a sphere for protection. They also have fewer body segments than typical millipedes and lack the ability to produce defensive chemical secretions.
children.funFact: Despite being called millipedes, Polyzoniidae members have far fewer than 1,000 legs - most species have only about 30-40 legs total due to their reduced number of body segments.

children.description: Polyzoniida are small, cylindrical millipedes that look like tiny pill bugs when they roll into a tight ball for protection. These gentle decomposers spend their lives in leaf litter and soil, slowly breaking down dead plant material with their small but effective jaws. They're among the smaller millipedes you might encounter, typically measuring less than an inch long.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipede orders, Polyzoniida have bodies that are perfectly suited for rolling into a complete sphere, with specialized body segments that fit together like puzzle pieces when curled up.
children.funFact: When threatened, these millipedes can roll into such a perfect ball that they're sometimes mistaken for seeds or small pebbles by both predators and curious nature explorers.

children.name: Polyxenida
Polyxenidae
Polyxenus
children.description: Polyxenus is a genus of tiny millipedes that are quite different from the typical cylindrical millipedes most people know. These small creatures have flattened, oval-shaped bodies covered in distinctive bristle-like hairs that give them a fuzzy appearance. They're among the smallest millipedes you'll encounter, usually measuring less than half an inch long.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipedes with hard, smooth segments, Polyxenus millipedes are covered in rows of bristles and have a distinctly flattened body shape rather than the typical rounded, worm-like form. They also have fewer body segments than most other millipede groups.
children.funFact: When threatened, bristly millipedes can detach some of their bristles, which stick to predators and may help them escape - similar to how some lizards drop their tails!

children.description: Polyxenidae are small, soft-bodied millipedes that look quite different from typical millipedes. Instead of the hard, shiny segments we usually associate with millipedes, these tiny creatures are covered in tufts of bristly hairs that give them a fuzzy, almost caterpillar-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipedes with hard exoskeletons, polyxenids have soft bodies covered in dense bristles and hairs. They also lack the ability to coil into a tight spiral like most millipedes do when threatened.
children.funFact: These millipedes are so small and secretive that many people have never seen one, despite them living in leaf litter and under logs throughout New England forests.

children.description: Bristle millipedes are small, soft-bodied millipedes that look quite different from their hard-shelled relatives. Instead of the typical rigid segments, they have a fuzzy appearance due to clusters of bristles (called tufts) covering their backs. These tiny creatures are among the most primitive millipedes and are often found in leaf litter and under bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other millipedes with hard, calcified exoskeletons, bristle millipedes have soft bodies covered in distinctive bristle tufts that give them a fuzzy, caterpillar-like appearance. They also lack the ability to coil into a tight spiral like many other millipedes.
children.funFact: When threatened, bristle millipedes can actually shed their bristle tufts as a defense mechanism, similar to how some lizards drop their tails!

children.name: Spirobolida
Rhinocricidae
Anadenobolus
children.description: Anadenobolus is a genus of large, colorful millipedes that are native to tropical regions but have established populations in some temperate areas. These millipedes are known for their striking yellow and black banding patterns and their relatively large size compared to most other millipedes found in North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their bright warning coloration of yellow and black stripes, which advertises their ability to secrete defensive chemicals when threatened.
children.funFact: The Bumblebee Millipede gets its name from its resemblance to a bumblebee due to its yellow and black striped pattern, which serves as a warning to predators about its toxic defensive secretions.

children.description: Rhinocricidae is a family of large, cylindrical millipedes that are among the most impressive arthropods you might encounter in New England forests. These gentle giants have segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per segment and feed on decaying plant material, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other millipedes by their relatively large size, robust build, and specific arrangements of reproductive structures and defensive glands.
children.funFact: When threatened, these millipedes can coil into a tight spiral and release a defensive chemical secretion that deters predators but is harmless to humans.

children.description: Iron millipedes are large, cylindrical millipedes that get their name from their hard, armor-like exoskeleton that often has a dark, metallic appearance. These impressive arthropods can grow quite large compared to other millipedes and are known for their ability to coil into tight spirals when threatened. They play important roles as decomposers, feeding on decaying plant material on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Iron millipedes are distinguished from other millipede groups by their robust, heavily armored body segments and their characteristic ability to form tight, neat coils when disturbed. Their exoskeleton is notably harder and more metallic-looking than most other millipede families.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating name and armor-like appearance, iron millipedes are completely harmless vegetarians that help recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead leaves and wood.

children.name: Lithobiomorpha
Lithobiidae
Lithobius
children.description: Typical Stone Centipedes are fast-moving predators that live under rocks, logs, and leaf litter throughout New England. These arthropods have 15 pairs of long legs and are skilled hunters that feed on small insects, spiders, and other invertebrates. They're among the most commonly encountered centipedes in our region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipede families, Lithobius species have exactly 15 pairs of legs as adults and relatively short antennae. Their bodies are flattened and well-adapted for squeezing into tight spaces under stones and debris.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they live on stones, these centipedes actually prefer moist environments and will quickly dry out if exposed to direct sunlight for too long.

children.name: Bothropolys
children.description: Bothropolys is a genus of centipedes known for their elongated bodies and numerous pairs of legs. These predatory arthropods are soil-dwelling creatures that hunt small invertebrates in leaf litter and underground burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive arrangement of sensory organs and the specific pattern of their leg segments. They have relatively robust bodies compared to some other centipede groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'hundred-leggers,' Bothropolys centipedes actually have far fewer than 100 legs, typically ranging from 30 to 60 legs depending on their age and species.

children.description: Lithobiidae are swift-moving centipedes commonly known as stone centipedes because they're often found hiding under rocks, logs, and leaf litter. These active predators have exactly 15 pairs of legs and are among the most commonly encountered centipedes in New England forests and gardens. They hunt small insects and other invertebrates, using their speed and venomous front claws to capture prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stone centipedes can be distinguished from other centipede families by their 15 pairs of long, slender legs and their relatively flattened body shape. Unlike house centipedes, they have shorter antennae and lack the extremely long, delicate legs.
children.funFact: Stone centipedes can live for several years and will autotomize (deliberately shed) their legs when grabbed by a predator, allowing them to escape while the detached leg continues to twitch and distract the attacker.

children.name: Henicopidae
Lamyctes
children.description: Lamyctes is a genus of small centipedes that are well-adapted to life in soil and leaf litter. These arthropods are predators that hunt tiny insects and other small invertebrates in dark, moist environments beneath the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have a distinctive appearance with relatively short antennae and a flattened body shape that helps them navigate through tight spaces in soil and decomposing organic matter.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'one-eyed centipede,' Lamyctes emarginatus actually has clusters of simple eyes on each side of its head that can detect light and dark but cannot form clear images.

children.name: Zygethobius
children.description: Zygethobius is a small genus of ground beetles that belongs to the family Carabidae. These tiny predatory beetles are specialized hunters that live in soil and leaf litter, where they feed on even smaller invertebrates like springtails and mites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size (typically less than 2mm long) and their pale, often translucent coloration that helps them blend into their underground habitat.
children.funFact: Despite being among the smallest ground beetles, Zygethobius species are fierce predators that can take down prey nearly as large as themselves using their powerful jaws.

children.description: Henicopidae is a family of soil-dwelling centipedes that are commonly found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist terrestrial habitats. These arthropods are characterized by having 15 pairs of legs as adults and relatively short antennae compared to other centipede families. They are active predators that hunt small invertebrates in the soil and forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other centipede families, henicopids have exactly 15 pairs of legs and lack eyes entirely, relying instead on their antennae and other sensory structures to navigate their dark underground world.
children.funFact: Despite being blind, henicopid centipedes are excellent hunters that can track down prey using vibrations and chemical cues detected through specialized sensory organs on their antennae.

children.description: Stone centipedes are fast-moving predators that live under rocks, logs, and leaf litter throughout New England's forests and gardens. These flattened, brownish arthropods have exactly 15 pairs of legs and hunt for small insects, spiders, and other prey in dark, moist places. They're among the most common centipedes you'll encounter when flipping over stones or rotting wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stone centipedes always have exactly 15 pairs of legs, distinguishing them from house centipedes (which have 15 pairs but are much more delicate) and soil centipedes (which can have many more leg pairs). Their bodies are notably flattened and they have relatively long antennae compared to other centipede groups.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they live on stones, stone centipedes are actually excellent climbers that can scale vertical surfaces and even run upside-down on ceilings when hunting prey.

children.name: Geophilomorpha
Geophilidae
Strigamia
children.description: Strigamia is a genus of soil-dwelling centipedes that spend their lives burrowing through earth and leaf litter. These slender, worm-like creatures are blind and rely on their sensitive antennae to navigate their underground world. They are active predators that hunt small invertebrates in the dark spaces between soil particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other centipedes, Strigamia species are completely eyeless and have a distinctly elongated, thread-like body that's perfectly adapted for squeezing through tight soil spaces.
children.funFact: Strigamia centipedes are among the few centipedes that provide parental care - mothers coil around their eggs and young to protect them from predators and fungi.

children.name: Henia
children.description: Henia is a genus of small, soil-dwelling centipedes that are found in various parts of the world. These centipedes are typically slender and pale-colored, living in the upper layers of soil and leaf litter where they hunt for tiny prey like mites and springtails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Henia can be distinguished from other centipede genera by their distinctive white or pale striping patterns and their relatively small size, usually measuring less than an inch in length.
children.funFact: Despite being called the White-Striped Centipede, Henia vesuviana was first discovered near Mount Vesuvius in Italy, giving it its volcanic species name.

children.name: Geophilus
children.description: Compost centipedes are slender, worm-like predators that spend their lives underground in soil and leaf litter. These pale yellow centipedes are perfectly adapted for life in tight spaces, with flexible bodies that can squeeze through tiny gaps between soil particles as they hunt for small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipedes, Geophilus species have extremely long, thin bodies with 49-57 pairs of legs and lack eyes completely. Their bodies are much more flexible and worm-like compared to the flattened house centipedes or robust stone centipedes found in New England.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'centipedes' (meaning 100 feet), these soil dwellers actually have between 98-114 legs, and they're one of the few centipede groups that can regenerate lost body segments!

children.description: Geophilidae are soil-dwelling centipedes that spend most of their lives underground, burrowing through dirt and leaf litter in search of small prey. These elongated arthropods have numerous body segments and legs, giving them a worm-like appearance that helps them navigate through tight spaces in the soil. They are important predators in the underground ecosystem, feeding on tiny insects, worms, and other soil creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipede families, geophilids have extremely long, thread-like bodies with many more segments than their relatives - often 40 or more pairs of legs compared to just 15 pairs in house centipedes. They also lack eyes and have relatively short antennae, adaptations for their subterranean lifestyle.
children.funFact: Some geophilid centipedes are among the 'leggiest' animals on Earth, with certain species having over 170 pairs of legs - that's more than 340 individual legs on a single creature smaller than your finger!

children.name: Schendylidae
Schendyla
children.description: Schendyla is a genus of small, slender centipedes that live in soil and leaf litter. These many-legged predators have elongated bodies and hunt tiny invertebrates in the dark spaces beneath the forest floor. They are part of the geophilomorph centipedes, which are specially adapted for life underground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Schendyla can be distinguished from other soil centipedes by their relatively small size and specific arrangement of body segments. They typically have fewer than 50 pairs of legs, unlike some other geophilomorph centipedes that can have over 100 pairs.
children.funFact: Despite being predators, Schendyla centipedes are so small that they primarily hunt microscopic soil animals like springtails and mites, making them important but nearly invisible members of the soil ecosystem.

children.description: Schendylidae is a family of soil-dwelling centipedes that are among the smallest members of the centipede world. These tiny predators live in the upper layers of soil and leaf litter, where they hunt for even smaller invertebrates like springtails and mites. They are part of the geophilomorph centipedes, which are known for their worm-like appearance and ability to burrow through soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their extremely small size (often less than 10mm long) and relatively few body segments compared to other soil centipedes. They also have distinctive arrangements of sensory organs on their antennae that help them navigate their underground world.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Schendylidae centipedes are fierce predators that can tackle prey nearly their own size using their venomous fangs.

children.description: Soil centipedes are long, thin predators that spend their lives underground, hunting for small prey in the dark spaces between soil particles. Unlike other centipedes, they have many more body segments and legs - often over 100 legs total - giving them their distinctive worm-like appearance. These secretive arthropods are perfectly adapted for life in tight underground spaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Soil centipedes have the most body segments of any centipede group, with 27 to 191 pairs of legs, and lack eyes completely since they live in perpetual darkness underground. Their bodies are much more flexible and elongated than other centipedes, allowing them to navigate through narrow soil crevices.
children.funFact: Some soil centipedes can live for up to 6 years and are among the few centipedes that care for their eggs and young, with mothers coiling around their eggs to protect them from fungi and predators.

children.name: Scolopendromorpha
Cryptopidae
Cryptops
children.description: Cave centipedes are small, pale predatory arthropods that belong to the genus Cryptops. These soil-dwelling hunters have 21 pairs of legs and are well-adapted to life in dark, moist environments like caves, basements, and underground spaces. They actively hunt small insects and other invertebrates using their venomous front claws.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other centipedes, cave centipedes have relatively short antennae and lack eyes, making them well-suited for navigating in complete darkness. Their pale coloration and compact body shape help distinguish them from the longer, more colorful centipedes found above ground.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cave centipedes,' these creatures commonly live in the dark spaces of human homes, particularly in basements and crawl spaces where they hunt for household pests.

children.description: Bark centipedes are small, flattened predators that live under loose bark, stones, and leaf litter where they hunt for tiny insects and other small prey. These centipedes have relatively few leg pairs compared to their larger cousins, typically sporting 21 pairs of legs as adults. They're well-adapted for squeezing into tight spaces in search of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike house centipedes with their long, spindly legs, bark centipedes have short, sturdy legs and a flattened body perfect for navigating narrow crevices. They also lack eyes, relying instead on their antennae and other senses to navigate their dark world.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bark' centipedes, many species in this family have adapted to cave life and have become completely blind, using vibrations and chemical cues to hunt in total darkness.

children.name: Scolopocryptopidae
Scolopocryptops
children.description: Red Centipedes (Scolopocryptops) are soil-dwelling arthropods characterized by their reddish-brown coloration and flattened bodies. These predatory creatures have 21 pairs of legs and are active hunters that feed on small insects, worms, and other invertebrates in the leaf litter and upper soil layers. They are part of the larger group of centipedes but represent a distinct genus with specific anatomical features.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other centipedes, Scolopocryptops species have a distinctive reddish color and relatively robust build. They can be distinguished from other centipede genera by their specific leg count of 21 pairs and their particular head shape and antenna structure.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they have 100 legs, Red Centipedes actually have exactly 42 legs (21 pairs), and unlike millipedes, they move with a distinctive undulating motion that helps them navigate quickly through soil and debris.

children.description: Scolopocryptopid centipedes are soil-dwelling predators that hunt small invertebrates in leaf litter and underground burrows. These medium-sized centipedes have long, flexible bodies with 21 pairs of legs and are adapted for life in moist forest environments. They play an important role as predators in woodland ecosystems throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike house centipedes with their extremely long legs, scolopocryptopids have shorter, more uniform legs along their body. They can be distinguished from stone centipedes by having 21 pairs of legs instead of 15 pairs.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'red centipedes,' many species in this family are actually more orange or reddish-brown in color, and they can live for several years underground.

children.name: Scolopendridae
Rhysida
children.description: Rhysida is a genus of large, tropical centipedes that are impressive predators in their ecosystems. These centipedes are characterized by their robust build and distinctive coloration, typically featuring dark bodies with contrasting colored legs. They are active hunters that prey on insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rhysida centipedes are distinguished from other centipede genera by their relatively thick, sturdy bodies and the distinctive blue or bluish coloration on their legs, which gives species like the Minor Blueleg Centipede their common name.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'centipedes' (meaning 100 feet), Rhysida species actually have exactly 21 pairs of legs, and no centipede species actually has 100 legs!

children.description: Scolopendrid centipedes are large, robust predatory arthropods that are among the most impressive centipedes in the world. They have powerful jaws and can deliver a painful bite, making them formidable hunters of insects, spiders, and other small animals. These centipedes prefer warm, humid environments and are typically found under logs, rocks, or in soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scolopendrids are distinguished from other centipede families by their large size, robust build, and particularly strong, well-developed poison claws. They also have fewer body segments than many other centipede groups, typically ranging from 21-23 pairs of legs.
children.funFact: Some tropical scolopendrid species can grow over a foot long and are capable of catching and eating small vertebrates like lizards, frogs, and even bats!

children.description: Tropical Centipedes are the largest and most robust centipedes you'll encounter, with powerful bodies designed for hunting other arthropods. These predatory creatures have exactly 21 or 23 pairs of legs and are equipped with strong jaws and venom to subdue their prey. While called 'tropical,' a few hardy species have made their way into New England's warmer microclimates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipede groups, Tropical Centipedes have a fixed number of leg pairs (either 21 or 23) and possess especially large, powerful front claws called forcipules for capturing prey. They also have more robust body segments and stronger exoskeletons compared to their more delicate centipede relatives.
children.funFact: Some Tropical Centipedes are caring parents - the females coil around their eggs to protect them and will clean them regularly to prevent fungal growth, which is quite unusual behavior for arthropods!

children.name: Scutigeromorpha
Scutigeridae
Scutigera
children.description: Scutigera is a genus of fast-moving centipedes known for their distinctive long, delicate legs and ability to live alongside humans. These arthropods are skilled hunters that use their speed and agility to catch small insects and spiders in dark, damp places like basements and bathrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipedes, Scutigera species have exceptionally long, thread-like legs that get progressively longer toward the back of their body, giving them a distinctive flowing appearance when they move.
children.funFact: House centipedes can live for several years and are actually beneficial roommates, as they hunt and eat many common household pests like cockroaches, silverfish, and flies.

children.name: Thereuonema
children.description: Thereuonema is a small genus of house centipedes that are native to East Asia but have been accidentally introduced to other parts of the world through human activity. These centipedes are characterized by their long, delicate legs and ability to live comfortably in human dwellings, where they hunt small insects and spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Thereuonema can be distinguished from other house centipedes by their relatively smaller size and specific leg segment arrangements, along with subtle differences in their body segmentation patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'Japanese House Centipede,' Thereuonema tuberculata is actually beneficial to have around your home since it actively hunts pest insects like cockroaches, silverfish, and flies.

children.description: Typical house centipedes are distinctive arthropods with extremely long, delicate legs that can span several inches across. They have 15 pairs of legs as adults and are known for their incredible speed, able to dart across walls and ceilings with remarkable agility. These centipedes are common household inhabitants that hunt other small arthropods like spiders, silverfish, and cockroaches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other centipedes, house centipedes have exceptionally long, thread-like legs that are much longer than their body length, and they retain all 15 pairs of legs throughout their adult life. Their legs are also notably fragile and will readily break off when grabbed by predators.
children.funFact: House centipedes can live for several years and continue to molt and regenerate lost legs even as adults, making them one of the few arthropods that can regrow limbs throughout their entire lifespan.

children.description: Long-legged centipedes are distinctive arthropods with extremely long, delicate legs that give them a spider-like appearance. Unlike other centipedes, they have only 15 pairs of legs as adults and can move with surprising speed and agility. These centipedes are active hunters that chase down their prey rather than burrowing through soil like most of their relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They stand out from other centipedes with their exceptionally long, thin legs that are much longer than their body segments, and their ability to run quickly across surfaces rather than crawling slowly underground.
children.funFact: House centipedes can live for several years and will actually groom their long legs one at a time, much like a cat cleaning itself!
